articles.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
articles.summary: His comments come as the government urged TikTok and other social media firms to remove wrong-way driving videos.
articles.body:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv, Burnham said the people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are "doing something that's truly reprehensible".

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.

It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.

The BBC has also contacted X for comment.

On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.

At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".

He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.

"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."

The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.

A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".

They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

articles.title: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
articles.summary: Business owners in both countries are navigating uncertainty and worry as the tit-for-tat import taxes ratchet up.
articles.body:
Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going.

Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glass and agates from her business, CindyLouWho2, based in Calgary, Alberta, come from Americans.

But after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed over the weekend and leaders of both countries pledged to slap 50% tariffs on each other's products, business owners on both sides of the border are bracing for the fallout.

With a majority of the items she sells falling under US President Donald Trump's newly imposed tariffs, Baldassi says she will need to add 50% to the price of most of her products to stay afloat.

"It's quite likely that it will wipe out most of my US sales," Baldassi told the BBC. "I expect that at least half of my business will be gone."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged levies starting on 8 September on US steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Trump tariffs went into effect on Saturday, hitting Canadian wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

In Canada, it is not clear how much more severe the impacts will be, since the country has grown somewhat used to the on-again-off-again trade war.

Lind Furniture has been in business for almost 60 years in the Canadian province of Ontario, selling leather furniture to big store clients like Sears and Costco over the years.

Sales dropped when Trump took office in 2025. "As soon as there were tariffs in the air, people put purchases on hold," Michael Saifer, general manager of Lind Furniture, told the BBC.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Now, his concern centres around Canadians' chances for victory.

"Everyone wants to sell to the Americans - they can buy from whoever they want," he said. "I don't know that we're going to win a war with them; we may get killed."

The US tariffs that took effect after talks broke off on Friday apply to about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian exports to the US - about 5% of what Canada ships to the US annually. The levies add to US tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

Canada would be very exposed if the import taxes multiply on both sides because 70% of its exports are to the US.

Navigating what comes next as both sides are dug in is proving a delicate balance for some business owners.

Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores.

Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff.

"If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said.

He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go.

"There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US.

"Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this."

'It's going to get worse before it gets better'

The impacts are not only being felt north of the US-Canada border. Carney promised his tariffs hitting US products in September will match Trump's "dollar-for-dollar". Details of the countermeasures will be released in the coming days, he said.

For Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing, a clothing store in Portland, Oregon, that means preparing for one of their best-selling items to potentially increase sizably in price.

Osgood creates designs that she has a Montreal-based company transfer onto pillows the couple sells in their store.

Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC.

"Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said.

The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said.

While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies.

Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol.

He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to.

"The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.

And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border.

The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state.

The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric".

"We completely understood that," she said.

But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat.

And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear.

"It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."

articles.title: US military says strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat kills two
articles.summary: US Southern Command says Sunday’s strike targeted vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes.
articles.body:
The United States military said it struck a suspected drug-trafficking boat in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people.

In a Monday post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said Sunday’s strike targeted a vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific.

“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking,” SOUTHCOM added.

“This operation is a clear and decisive reminder that SOUTHCOM is taking the fight directly to the cartels.”

Grainy, black-and-white video accompanying the post appeared to show a boat moving through the water immediately before a large explosion.

The post stated that under the direction of SOUTHCOM Commander General Francis L. Donovan, the Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on the low-profile vessel.

“We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists — disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” Donovan was quoted as saying.

“Let me be clear, we will not permit narco-terrorists to operate with impunity in the Western Hemisphere, nor will we allow their deadly poison to reach American communities. This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the U.S. homeland.”

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in early September, with President Donald Trump arguing that Washington is effectively at war with Latin American drug cartels.

Since then, more than 200 people have been killed in strikes across the Eastern Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, according to a tally by the AFP news agency.

However, the Trump administration has not provided definitive evidence that the targeted vessels were involved in drug trafficking.

Legal experts and rights groups warn that the attacks could amount to extrajudicial killings.

The Pentagon’s inspector general said in May that it would review whether the military followed standard targeting procedures, though the evaluation will not examine the legal authority behind the strikes.

articles.title: Gen Z grew up as the rash guard generation. So why are so many skipping sunscreen in pursuit of the perfect tan?
articles.summary: Gen Z knows skipping sun protection to get a tan is risky. Some are doing it anyway.
articles.body:
Gen Z grew up with parents who learned about sun safety the hard way, after spending their own youth coated in baby oil — or SPF 4 at best — and lying out in the backyard or baking in tanning beds. But as the saying goes, "When you know better, do better." And they did: shimmying their children into rash guards at the pool or beach and regularly slathering and spraying them with sunscreen.

Gen Z, it seemed, was on track to become the most sun-safe generation yet. But now that they're in their teens and 20s, some are deliberately "tanmaxxing," side-eying — or outright skipping — sun protection and falling for sunscreen myths online. A 2024 American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) survey found that nearly 30% of Gen Z respondents said getting a tan was a higher priority than preventing skin cancer.

So what happened to the "rash guard generation"?

For a clue, look no further than Gen Z's social media feeds. That's where you'll find teens and young adults sharing their tanning tips — and even proudly showing off noticeable tan lines , something previous generations went out of their way to avoid.

Brooklyn (aka Brookie) Marie Win is one of them. Amid her multi-step skin care regimen and GRWM (get ready with me) videos, Win recently broke down her "fool-proof" tanning routine to her 230k followers, showing how to get "amazing, crisp" tan lines like hers. All you need is a triangle bikini — leave the sunscreen at home. "If you want me to be honest, I don't use SPF. I know I should," she says, before listing some sunscreen recommendations for followers who do. She then shares the tanning oil and gel she swears by, along with a cheaper trick: misting yourself with water.

Other TikTokers are co-opting the UV index — which measures the strength of the sun's ultraviolet (UV) radiation on a scale of 0 to 11 (the higher the number, the greater potential for UV damage) — to identify the "ideal" times to tan , instead of using it as intended: to know when to protect your skin from the sun. There are even apps like SunSafe and Sun Tracker: UV Index and Tan to make this easier, under the misguided pretense of a "safe tan."

Still others are questioning whether sunscreen itself is safe, including buying into the debunked claim that it can cause cancer . TikTok user Alicia Hally, for example, posted : "The sun gives you cancer. Sunscreen gives you cancer. We die either way so you may as well be tanned xx." (One response: "I'm trying to figure out if this is rage bait or not.")

Sunscreen misinformation aside, many, like Lauren Nagyvary, know that the real risk is using little to no sun protection — but they're doing it anyway. "I will only tan when I have no SPF on at all," Nagyvary says on her TikTok . "I'm not telling you this is good or bad advice, but if you want to tan easier, maybe just don't wear SPF and just stay out less. But again, I know that probably like increases your risk of skin cancer. I just feel like it's more efficient."

That contradiction is particularly surprising for a generation known for its fixation on wellness, longevity and elaborate anti-aging skin care routines. And it's not as if Gen Z missed the memo on sun damage: They've spent their entire lives hearing about the importance of sun protection from their parents, doctors and more recently, social media.

"Unlike many who experienced tanning culture in the 1970s and 1980s, Gen Z has grown up in an era when the link between UV exposure and skin cancer has been widely shared with the public," Dr. Elizabeth K. Hale , a dermatologist and senior vice president of The Skin Cancer Foundation, tells Yahoo. "But, unfortunately, tanning culture continues to make a resurgence despite best efforts to keep the public educated about their risk for developing skin cancer, as well as the risk of premature skin aging."

There are several reasons, say experts. One is that it's hard to resist a pervasive beauty trend — in this case, being tan. Bronzed skin "is often associated with looking healthy, fit or fresh from vacation," says dermatologist Dr. Annette Czernik . "There is also a natural tendency when we are young to place more value on how something makes us look or feel today than on a health consequence decades away. So even a generation that understands the science can still be pulled toward a trend that offers an immediate cosmetic reward."

But appearances can be deceiving. "A tan is a sign of UV damage, not healthy skin," Dr. Supriya Rastogi , a dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group, tells Yahoo.

Social media can also make even harmful behaviors seem normal when you see them over and over again, explains Sanam Hafeez , a neuropsychologist and director of Comprehend the Mind. "If someone's feed is filled with influencers tanning on vacation, using tanning beds or showing off very bronzed skin, that look can quickly become familiar," she says. "The brain can start interpreting that repetition as evidence that 'everyone is doing it,' even when that is not actually true." Likes, comments and compliments help reinforce the behavior "by attaching a social reward to the appearance," she points out.

As anyone who spends enough time on social media knows, questionable health claims and dubious advice are everywhere — and sun protection is no exception. A 2026 AAD survey found that 64% of Gen Z respondents reported encountering sunscreen misinformation online. "Gen Z has grown up with unprecedented access to information, but that access also means that they are constantly exposed to unverified claims, opinions and misinformation," says Hale. "Social media can make it difficult to distinguish evidence-based health information from content that is simply popular or persuasive."

Hale points to a June 2026 study that found misinformation receives much higher audience engagement . "This really shows us how someone today might see a false sunscreen claim repeatedly from different influencers and begin to assume it must be true, even when the claim is not supported by scientific evidence," she says.

Rastogi agrees. "Social media can make personal experiences and influencer claims feel just as credible as medical advice, especially when misinformation is presented in a convincing or relatable way," she says.

One of the issues with tanning is that it feeds into our "get it now, pay later" culture. In this case, the "payoff" — bronzed skin — is immediate, while the consequences, like premature aging and skin cancer, can take years or even decades to surface. "The problem is that UV damage builds quietly in the skin and may not become noticeable for years," says Czernik.

Hafeez says that can create a false sense of safety. "Someone may tan repeatedly and think, 'Nothing bad happened last time,'" she notes. That thinking is especially true for teens and 20-somethings for whom health consequences years down the road can sound like a "future me" problem.

However, some creators are starting to post about the consequences of skipping sunscreen and using the UV index as a tanning tool.

"The time 2 years ago i thought it was a good idea to spend 3 hours in UV 11 'tanning' with no sunscreen," posted TikTok user Cathryn Akers , revealing the blistering sunburn she developed on her face. Several people in the comments called it a "lifechanging sunburn" — and not in a good way. "I had a life changing sunburn like this in high school. I'm now 23 with melanoma," one person commented.

TikToker Kelly Trebendis shared her bright red sunburn after using tanning oil on the beach while the UV index was 8. She tried to head off criticism by captioning the video: "I know I'm stupid you don't have to tell me I'm so mad at myself." That didn't stop commenters from sounding the alarm and even sharing their own skin cancer experiences, including photos.

So what should Gen Z know before trying to chase a tan? For starters, experts emphasize that sunscreen isn't the danger — UV exposure is.

"There's no good evidence that sunscreen, when used as directed, causes cancer in humans," says Czernik. "Overwhelming evidence shows that sunscreen helps reduce the risk of certain skin cancers by protecting from UV radiation."

And while some chemical sunscreen ingredients may enter the bloodstream, Czernik says research hasn't shown that this is harmful. Still concerned? Mineral-based sunscreen with zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide mostly sits on the skin's surface and is generally considered very safe.

And sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher isn't your only line of defense. Experts also recommend seeking shade during peak sun hours (between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.); wearing a hat and sunglasses; choosing clothing with UPF 50+ , which is designed to block UV rays; and spending less time outside when UV levels are especially high — in other words, using the UV index as intended.

Swapping the sun for a tanning bed isn't a safer bet either. Hale notes that they can emit UVA radiation at levels up to 10 to 15 times stronger than the midday sun, and research shows that using a tanning bed just once before age 35 is linked to a 75% increase in melanoma risk .

"The bottom line is: There is no such thing as a safe tan," says Hale. "Protecting your skin now can help reduce the amount of UV damage you accumulate throughout your lifetime."

And if it's the bronzed look you're after, Rastogi suggests reaching for spray tans or self-tanners instead. "Ultimately, when it comes to your skin, it's best to look beyond social media trends and rely on evidence-based advice from dermatologists," she says.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ on Iran puts China in the crosshairs
articles.summary: President Trump’s announcement of a major economic warfare campaign against Iran also has the effect of putting China in the crosshairs, the Islamic republic’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports. Trump’s threats to go after any country, business or banking institution supporting Iran come as diplomatic efforts have unraveled, six months…
articles.body:
President Trump’s announcement of a major economic warfare campaign against Iran also has the effect of putting China in the crosshairs, the Islamic republic’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports.

Trump’s threats to go after any country, business or banking institution supporting Iran come as diplomatic efforts have unraveled, six months of military pressure have failed to cow the Islamic republic and transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains a dangerous gamble.

While Trump held back from calling out China specifically in a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was blunt, calling for the Chinese “to get with the program.”

“We are confident that everyone wants the strait reopened and for energy prices to come back down … keep in mind that the Chinese get 50 percent — 5-0 — of their energy from inside, from the gulf. So it would do them a big service to get with the program,” he said Thursday in an interview with CNBC.

Bessent said he will hold a press conference Monday to detail the administration’s game plan.

“Sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. China calls on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said when asked by Bloomberg about the impact on China.

Analysts are cautious on whether Trump’s threats of economic “D-Day” against Iran and its enablers will bear fruit — and whether the president is determined to follow through with punishing economic actions against China ahead of a state visit for President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24.

Trump is eager for China to follow through on buying American agriculture, Boeing jets and U.S. oil, as well as preserve American access to Beijing’s supply of critical minerals — essential components of U.S. weapons production that have been depleted by the war.

“A much larger move against China one month before a leader-level summit in Washington would carry real diplomatic risk, invite a Chinese counterresponse and potentially put the meeting itself under pressure,” said Craig Singleton, senior fellow at the nonpartisan Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Trump imposed earlier sanctions against so-called Chinese teapot refineries — small-to-medium independent plants processing Iranian oil — as part of the economic pressure campaign against Tehran. But Beijing rejected those sanctions and told blacklisted refineries to ignore the U.S. penalties.

“If the administration is unwilling to target the larger Chinese entities and financial channels sustaining Iranian trade, it is hard to see sanctions alone bringing Tehran to its knees,” Singleton continued.

He pointed to Russia as an example. While broad, international sanctions have imposed economic hardship, Moscow has demonstrated resilience by relying heavily on countries — like China — holding back sanctions to avoid economic collapse.

“‘Economic D-Day’ sounds dramatic, but it may say more about shrinking options than expanding leverage,” Singleton said.

“The military campaign has produced diminishing returns, so Trump is pivoting from missiles to markets. The harder question is whether Washington is actually willing to impose costs on major Chinese actors and risk disrupting the trade truce before the summit.”

Likewise, Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran, said the administration’s sanctions are a very strong warning to China and its banks enabling Iran, but “the proof will be in the follow-through and enforcement.”

And Josh Lipsky, vice president and chair in international economics at the Atlantic Council, told Bloomberg News that Trump’s threats against Iran are likely to fall flat absent close coordination with Europe and Chinese banks willing to cut off Tehran. He also raised both Trump’s and Xi’s desires for a good visit in September.

“It’s unclear to me how we’re going to choke off Iran more than we have financially without triggering immense blowback from China on the eve of President Xi’s visit to Washington, which has been so carefully choreographed over many months now,” he said.

The last face-to-face between Trump and Xi occurred in May in Beijing. The summit was regarded as successful in maintaining relationship stability and avoiding major ruptures. The leaders discussed the U.S. war against Iran, and Trump told reporters at the time that Xi said he feels strongly that Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon — one of the administration’s stated priorities for starting the war on Feb. 28 — “and he wants them to open up the strait.”

The six-month war in the Middle East is a burden on China. In June, Iranian oil imports to China hit a historic low, dropping to below 800,000 barrels per day, Reuters reported , citing data from ship-tracking company Vortexa.

Oil is only one part of the trade relationship between Iran and China, with Tehran relying on Chinese technology exports being critical to building its drone and missile programs. The U.S. bars the sale of such components to Iran.

The U.S. has blacklisted 366 entities based in China and Hong Kong for evading sanctions on Iran, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission wrote in a March fact sheet.

The fact sheet also noted a network of front companies and small regional banks in China and Hong Kong helps Iran launder most of the renminbi — Chinese currency — proceeds from the oil sales into the global financial system.

But the disruption in global energy supplies, rising inflation and knock-on effects to supply-chain networks impact China’s push to see the U.S.-Iran war resolved.

“China has powerful incentives to see the conflict end as quickly as possible,” wrote Zhao Long, director and senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, in an article for the Brookings Institution.

But while China helped push Iran to a ceasefire with the U.S. in April, there are few signals that Beijing wants to intervene again.

“When a conflict involves major military powers and China is not the cause of the war or a party to it, Beijing generally sees neither a particular responsibility nor a realistic possibility of becoming the primary mediator,” Zhao wrote.

articles.title: Baker busts common sourdough myth that keeps busy Americans out of the kitchen
articles.summary: Kate Freebairn's debut cookbook "Easy Sourdough on Any Schedule" shows how sourdough bread baking fits into busy lives with minimal hands-on time.
articles.body: A loaf of sourdough can take three days to make. That doesn't mean you'll spend three days making it. That's the distinction Kate Freebairn wants busy would-be bread bakers to understand. Freebairn, a sourdough recipe developer and food blogger in rural Western Australia, says one of the biggest barriers keeping beginners away from sourdough is the perception that making it will take over their lives. COSTCO SHOPPERS DIVIDED OVER NEW 'SOURDOUGH' BREAD AS CRITICS SAY IT'S NOT THE REAL THING "I think that people think that sourdough is really difficult and that it takes a lot of time, but really, even though a loaf of sourdough might take three days to complete, the actual time that you'll have your hands in the dough might only be an hour," Freebairn told Fox News Digital. Her debut cookbook, "Easy Sourdough on Any Schedule," is built around fitting bread baking into everyday life rather than fitting life around bread baking. For someone working a typical weekday, Freebairn suggests feeding the starter before bed, mixing the dough over morning coffee and tending to it while the kids are having breakfast. The dough can ferment while its baker is at work, then be shaped and refrigerated that evening. The next morning, "you can wake up, pop the oven on, make your coffee and bake a fresh loaf of sourdough," Freebairn said. "So, the actual time that you have your hands in the dough is very minimal." Freebairn also points to potential health benefits as another reason to choose sourdough. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Because it is naturally fermented, she said, "the microbes in the sourdough starter, they're already doing some of the digestion for you," adding that sourdough "tends to not spike your blood sugar" and "has lots of prebiotics, which are really good for gut health." Her favorite benefit, however, is simpler. "Probably the best thing is it really does taste better," she said. Beginners don't need a kitchen full of specialized equipment, either. Freebairn said an old pickle jar can hold a starter, and an ordinary bowl can substitute for a proofing basket. Her own Dutch oven isn't an expensive status piece. "I literally still to this day use a $30 Dutch oven I bought from Aldi," she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Perhaps the bigger investment is patience. Freebairn recommends beginners expect their earliest loaves to be imperfect and says it may take five to 10 attempts to start getting the hang of the process. "There's a lesson in every loaf," she said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ It's advice that captures her approach to sourdough: Start with what you have, fit it around the life you're already living and don't worry if the first loaf isn't perfect. articles.title: ‘Aura farming’ began as a meme. Latin American youth have turned it into a competitive sport
articles.summary: “Aura battles” have taken off in Latin American countries in contests that appear to be designed for virality, with young competitors often demonstrating exaggerated versions of popular TikTok dance moves for the audience.
articles.body: A group of rowdy spectators gathers in a public square, encircling two young men facing each other with intense looks in their eyes. The crowd points their phones at the pair, who are alternating between short dances, rhythmic movements, and striking poses. This is not a scene from “Zoolander;” the crowd is attending a championship of “aura” in Costa Rica’s capital, San Jose, according to videos posted to TikTok and Instagram. Tuesday’s event at the University of Costa Rica is one of many so-called “aura battles” that have taken off in Latin American countries, including Mexico, Argentina, and Brazil. The contests appear to be designed for virality, with young competitors often demonstrating exaggerated versions of popular TikTok dance moves for the audience. Outrageousness seems to be the point of these battles, which have no apparent criteria, judges, or rules. Instead, contestants compete for crowd reaction and are rewarded with attention and, in some cases, small cash prizes. The phenomenon may have a special appeal to youth in the region due to a culture of assembling in public areas, Frederick Luis Aldama, a humanities professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told CNN. “These are definitely collective and public and person to person, and because in Latin America, we have a long history of the plaza, of the courtyard, of the gathering in the parks,” Aldama explained. They also provide a free, nonviolent space for youth to seek human connection among their peers and may reflect a desire to disconnect from technology and be present, he said. Aldama happened to witness one such “aura battle” in Mexico City’s Parque México. “What I noticed was completely against what I had been trained to think would be the winner, which is someone who was doing a more high-intensity kind of move,” he said. “I realized that the one that won was the one who just brought the kind of aura, the glow of absolute total composure.” Taking inspiration from ‘aura farming’ The battle’s precursor comes from “aura farming,” a term that has taken renewed meaning online in recent years. “Aura farming” is described by the Merriam Webster dictionary as “the act of doing something to look cool, impressive, stylish, etc., especially — and importantly — without trying too hard.” The phrase first surfaced in early 2024 and has grown in popularity since, according to Know Your Meme. It reached a wider audience the following year through viral videos featuring an 11-year-old Indonesian boy named Rayyan Arkan Dikha, dancing at the front of a boat. With a steely disposition, Dikha is seen in the videos standing at the very front of a thin boat, executing a repetitive series of dance moves as a line of rowers propel them through a river. As the videos quickly gained traction, commenters and other social media users remarked on the high levels of “aura” possessed by Dikha. Since then, Dikha has accrued thousands of followers on Instagram and was named a tourism ambassador for his home province of Riau. As his performance amassed millions of views, the term “aura farming” began frequently appearing across the internet: from video edits glorifying anime characters to X posts celebrating athletes or celebrities. ‘They become a character’ “Aura battles” have begun appearing in public spaces across Latin American countries, often organized by local content creators and engineered for maximum virality. Videos of the competitions have received hundreds of thousands of views on social media. Victor Gabriel Tourinho Camargo, a Brazilian content creator known as Uvitinho, organized several tournaments in the city of Suzano. More than 200 people participated, Uvitinho said. Videos showed the participants packed into a park, including one dressed as a sheikh with a briefcase full of Brazilian reais. “The aura farming championship was something created with the focus of taking something popular on the internet and bringing it to reality, mixing it with childhood games and showing people and children that there is still hope for a more real life with genuine moments,” Uvitinho told CNN. “There was a mix of shy, antisocial and extroverted people… and in that moment, they all put aside all that, played together, and made friends,” he added. Mexican YouTuber Alex Crashers described encountering an aura battle in Mexico in a video shared this week. “Even though it seems silly, I got hyped every time someone pulled off a new move,” he said. Argentinian content creator Cielo, known as Cieloween, helped organize an “aura battle” in Chinatown in Buenos Aires scheduled for this Saturday after watching viral videos of a previous battle in the coastal city of Mar del Plata just days before. “The concept of ‘aura farming’ has been around for a while, but now the competition aspect has started to take off,” she told CNN. In many ways, the events resemble past versions of youth “battles” in which competitors were equipped with Pokémon cards, Beyblades or rap verses. Cieloween explained that the moves shown by participants vary widely. “It depends on the person and what they want to show. Some are more serious, while others are more humorous and entertaining. It depends on the person and the character they want to portray, because ultimately, they become a character,” she said. Cieloween said she doesn’t know how many people will attend Saturday’s event, but that the goal is to build community. “That’s what it’s all about: meeting people, being together, connecting with people who share your interests. Making friends, laughing. That’s what we’re going for,” she said. But the showcase has also attracted skeptics. The battle at the University of Costa Rica gained significant attention, with some viewers leaving comments on the videos over the spectacle. In the Brazilian city of Cuiabá, the mayor, Abílio Brunini, prohibited one such championship from taking place in the city’s main public space. “I believe that, in the future, the people who participate in this game will feel very ashamed,” he said. Still, social media videos showed individuals defiantly competing in front of the City Hall building in July. Despite some derision, the competitions have continued as participants embrace the absurdity and young people seek connection. “All this stuff that’s thrown at them, having gone through lockdown, having been like pulled away from these so-called third spaces, these plazas, these places of engagement. No wonder it’s coming back like a storm,” Aldama, the University of Texas professor, told CNN. He compares the criticism to the backlash faced by the Australian breakdancer Raygun, who was mocked for her viral Olympic performance. “There’s always going to be that negativity,” Aldama said. “But what I saw and experienced was really working-class youth, especially in Latin America, gathering to celebrate something joyful.”

Participants gather for an open-air performance involving an exchange of movements, dance, acrobatics, physical feats, and gestures, each adapted to the individual's personality.

Armed with colourful oars, rowers pack into long boats in western Indonesia, paddling furiously in front of race crowds swelled by the viral success of a young boy famous for his dancing at the front of the traditional vessels.

articles.title: ‘A sucker born every minute’: The man who duped tourists with a fake Greek amphitheater
articles.summary: This “ancient Greek” stadium in northern Italy was charging locals €40. An investigation into it took only a day to conclude it was a scam.
articles.body: Of the eight TripAdvisor reviews of the amphitheater near Arcugnano, in Italy’s northern Veneto region, all give fulsome, five-star praise. “An enchanting place,” reads one review. “A world beyond space and time,” enthuses another. “Definitely one of the best places I have ever been to,” raves another. “Unique on the planet,” writes another visitor. That last one was prescient, because the theater certainly was unique. It wasn’t Greek, as it purported to be. It wasn’t even Roman. Instead, the “kind custodian” who was “more or less a historian, and an excellent narrator,” as one other visitor dubbed him, had built it himself. This month, after a 10-year legal battle, the owner has been jailed for forging works of art, carrying out building works without authorization, and destroying a protected landscape. The case has scandalized Italy, a country that just edges out China for the most UNESCO World Heritage sites and is home to many legitimate Greek and Roman theaters, from those of Syracuse and Pompeii, where productions are still staged each summer, to the amphitheater of Verona, 40 miles west of Arcugnano, which becomes a mega-stage for opera each summer. Franco Malosso, the owner, creator and self-styled discoverer of the nearly 54,000-square-foot “ancient” site, charged visitors up to 40 euros ($46) to visit the “theater” he had built from scratch. On a scenic hillside, employing a local construction firm, he had built seating and steps, which, according to evidence presented in court, he had artificially aged, then added a smattering of cement columns and plaster statues over the small “lake” that he had dug out himself. The traditional tiered seating, which he said had been built by hand by the ancient Greeks over 2,000 years ago, was constructed by 21st-century builders using machines. They used newly quarried stone from Puglia and cement, while a supporting wall was topped with polystyrene, according to court documents shared with CNN. “Just the idea of it is insane,” Darius Arya, archaeologist and director of Ancient Rome Live, told CNN, calling Malosso’s scheme “diabolical” and “terrible.” Malosso, according to evidence presented in court, is said to have hosted concerts and performances inside the site, which went by no fewer than three names: Anfiteatro Berico, Anfiteatro Marittimo Berico and Anfiteatro Porta degli Angeli. He also led guided visits around the site, according to prosecutors. For anyone with a basic knowledge of ancient history, there were red flags aplenty. Malosso’s building was a fan-shaped theater, not an amphitheater, which is oval. It wasn’t near the sea, as “Marittimo” implies — Arcugnano is around 50 miles from the coast. There wasn’t an ancient “Angels’ Gate” (Porta degli Angeli) at the site, either. Nor could it have been Greek — while northern Italy is replete with Roman remains, the ancient Greeks only colonized farther south. Not that the visitors, who raved about the concrete columns and chalk statues, seemed to have cared. Nor did they seem to notice that where there should have been a stage, Malosso — who also went by the name of Von Rosenfranz — had excavated a photogenic pool of water. “Why was there a pool of water there, there were no maritime performances,” said Arya. “It’s like a folly — it doesn’t feel right.” The dupe theater, on a hillside covered in protected woodland outside the small town of Arcugnano, just over three miles south of Vicenza, was discovered by local law enforcement, who immediately referred it to the cultural superintendency in October 2016. A site inspection was carried out by a representative of the local heritage board and police from the Carabinieri’s Nucleo Tutela Patrimonio Artistico (TPC), the division known in English as the “art squad” for its work investigating stolen artworks and forgeries. The theater was so clearly fake that the inspection was concluded in a single day, Lt. Col. Giuseppe Marseglia, commander of the TPC in Monza, which covers northern Italy, told CNN. Marseglia called it a “truly obscene” attempt at forgery. “Of all criminals, forgers are the ones with the most talent, because they are able to create works of art,” he said. “Then there are scammers … I have no respect [for Malosso]. Calling him a forger is an offense to forgers.” Marseglia said that in his 25 years in the force, he had never seen or heard of an entire archaeological site being faked. ‘Make it look old’ The theater was constructed on land that was part of the UNESCO-protected Berici Hills landscape. Malosso — who claimed to be the legal representative of the land owner, a business based in the British Virgin Islands — had originally applied for planning permission to build a garage, according to court documents. Instead, he hired local builders to construct the theater, instructing them to “make it look old,” according to one of them, who gave evidence in court. Prosecutors said he told visitors that he had discovered it after a landslide and advertised it to the public starting in 2014, including writing to the mayor of Arcugnano to explain how profitable the site could be. Ticket-holders were told that the site had been visited by Julius Caesar, Cleopatra, and Juliet Capulet, the fictional character invented by William Shakespeare. Unearthing the theater like Malosso claimed wouldn’t be reasonably possible, says Mauro Puddo, an archeologist specializing in the Roman world and researcher at the Università per Stranieri di Siena. According to Puddu, at the standard rate of excavation only a maximum of one row of seats per year could be revealed as part of an extensively planned and carefully monitored excavation. “You’re not allowed to dig up antiquities in your backyard,” Arya added. “You have to declare it, they investigate it, they excavate. This is terrible.” Visitors from out of town were charged 12 euros ($14), according to local media, while locals were disincentivized with a 40 euro ($46) charge. Private group tours were also reportedly available at a cost of 600 euros ($692) for 45 minutes. Marseglia said the charges were framed as a “minimum contribution for the upkeep of the site.” It is not known how many victims took the bait but the site was only reported to the authorities in 2016, two years after its opening. “I guess there’s a sucker born every minute, but I suppose when you have something advertised, people think this is the real deal,” said Arya. Malosso was convicted in 2019 and lost an initial appeal in 2020. He made a final appeal to the Corte di Cassazione, Italy’s supreme court, arguing — among other things — that his forgery was so obvious that nobody could have reasonably believed it to be true. The Cassazione rejected his arguments and reaffirmed the original sentence, which he is now serving, including a 28-month jail term and a fine of 3,000 euros ($3,462) plus 3,500 euros ($4,040) in legal fees. Since his original conviction, the law has been tightened to allow sentences of up to five years for forgery, said Marseglia. ‘Clearly modern’ Why Malosso embarked on his scheme is a mystery, experts told CNN. For starters, he apparently hadn’t done his homework. The ancient Greeks never colonized anywhere as far north as Vicenza, said Marseglia, who called it “crazy.” Arya was baffled at what the plan was. “You can tell it’s fake immediately,” he said. One photo from the site’s Facebook page shows a visibly cement column accompanied by a rather modern-looking sculpture of a man, which turned out to be made from plaster. “The columns are clearly modern,” said Peter Matthaes, director of Milan’s Museo di Arte e Scienza, which is partly dedicated to the art of forgery. Matthaes said that he thought perhaps Malosso’s skills as a raconteur could have swept visitors along. “From a few comments on the internet you realize that the visitors were accompanied by a narrator to turn the visit into an experience. How many times are we in front of this situation? How many times are we told a story — by advertisements, in politics or in the media trying to convince us of what is the ‘truth,’ when in reality the truth is something different?” ‘Grudging respect’ Malosso’s theater-amphitheater is hardly the first fake to hit the headlines, says Puddu, who points to the Renaissance-era Donation of Constantine — a forged Roman imperial decree that transferred imperial authority to the Pope — as the most famous fake of classical history. Rome’s Museo di Arte Salvata, or Museum of Rescued Art, exhibits both stolen and forged works of ancient art in an ancient Roman bathhouse, while Matthaes’ Museo di Arte e Scienza devotes an entire floor to archaeological and artistic forgery. Marseglia said that forgery of antiquities started in the Renaissance. Today, he said, a 15th-century forgery of a Roman medal would be more valuable than an actual Roman artifact. “It’s a very vast topic,” said Puddu. “I understand why archaeologists are horrified, but I understand why you might feel a grudging respect.” “Forgeries are a part of human civilization — we try to trick each other all the time,” he said. “A foundational text of humanity, the ‘Odyssey’ and also the ‘Iliad’ are based on a trick — an illusion, a forgery.” The site has now been sequestered and Malosso was ordered to tear down the theater, though its fate remains to be seen. Arya warned that it will be an expensive job. “I’d hate to think of seeing taxpayer money going to remove something like that,” he said. The mayor of Arcugnano recently told La Repubblica that he would not spend public money on it. He did not respond to a request for an interview from CNN. Nor did the attorney who represented Malosso in his supreme court appeal. His attorney from his original trial declined to comment. Actual Roman ruins As for those interested in seeing legitimate sites, Arya recommends Verona for an amphitheater, or Aquileia, two and a half hours northeast on Veneto’s border with Friuli. The Roman city is accompanied by a church with early Christian mosaics. The area around Arcugnano is rich in history, says Andrea Rosignoli, the superintendent for the Ministry of Culture for Vicenza. Within Arcugnano’s territory is the Lago di Fimon, which was once home to Neolithic stilted structures on the lakeside. The Berici Hills are home to various prehistoric caves, he said, recommending the Grotta di San Bernardino, while genuine Roman sites are on lower ground nearby. Rosignoli also recommended the Museo Civico Naturalistico-Archeologico in Vicenza, which has finds from Lake Fimon and Teatro Berga, an actual Roman theater that once stood in the city center. Meanwhile, for Puddu, two of the best-preserved Roman theaters are at Amman in Jordan and Orange, France. Closer to home, he recommends the one in Lecce, Puglia, which sits in the main square. In the meantime, in Arcugnano, the entrance to Malosso’s theater is still visible. A modern-looking stone wall and huge metal gate are accompanied by signs detailing the supposed history of the site. One mentions that the house where Juliet Capulet grew up is within the complex, including a balcony, with no reference to her being a fictional Shakespearean character. Another mentions an ancient burial site. Locals say that the theater used to be visible from the road below, but today it is covered entirely by thick undergrowth. If the plans to destroy the theater are followed through, the process will, ironically, have to start with an excavation. Only this time, a real one.

articles.title: Target reached for memorial to Channel Island WW2 journalists
articles.summary: Historian Timothy Crook says £1,000 has been raised for a memorial plaque to go in a London church.
articles.body:
A fundraising target for a memorial to Channel Islands journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two has been reached, organisers have said.

Historian Timothy Crook, who led the appeal , said the target of £1,000 was reached thanks to the "immense and wonderful generosity" of a gentleman who donated £775, plus £225 donated by members of the Chartered Institute of Journalists (CIoJ).

Journalists to be commemorated include Joseph Gillingham and Joseph Tierney who were arrested, deported and died in prison for sharing news heard on banned radios; and Frank Falla, who survived imprisonment and whose book The Silent War told how islanders challenged and outmanoeuvred censorship.

Crook, from the CIoJ, said it was hoped a plaque would be placed in St Bride's Church in Fleet Street, London, known as the "journalists' church".

Crook told BBC Jersey, if people worked in Fleet Street or around British journalism, they knew the church was something which commemorated "the courage and bravery" of those who sacrificed their lives "in the cause of their work".

"Current president Gerald Bowey is closely involved in it, and he's been very much involved in persuading the church to finally give national recognition to the enormously courageous journalists in the Channel Islands, and those ordinary people who became journalists who resisted occupation," Crook said.

He added: "When I worked in Fleet Street, I would often go to the church to say silent prayers, light candles, and remember people I've known in my career that go back 51 years in journalism that didn't come back."

Crook also thanked "brilliant historian" Prof Gilly Carr, whose "outstanding research" enabled them to recognise and appreciate the generation of journalists who achieved and "gave so much in those dark years" between 1940 and 1945.

Joe Gillingham, from Guernsey, and Joe Tierney, from Jersey, secretly spread news which often contradicted that put out through island newspapers, which were only allowed to carry war news provided and approved by German authorities.

Prof Carr said the journalists' stories were "well known" on the Channel Islands, but not so much in the UK.

She said it was great CIoJ was campaigning to have the memorial for the Channel Islanders in the church in London.

She said: "I think this memorial will be for quite a wider range of people, and I think anyone who knows grandparents might have kept a radio or who whispered the news to neighbours can feel themselves included in this because they were still spreading the news."

articles.title: UK woman whose life was âsavedâ by a cancer trial cycles 186 miles to thank the hospital that gave her hope
articles.summary: UK News: Julie Rose, a 49-year-old woman from Bridgwater, Somerset, has taken on a 186-mile cycle ride to The Royal Marsden in London after a clinical trial ga.
articles.body: Julie Rose, a 49-year-old woman from Bridgwater, Somerset, has taken on a 186-mile cycle ride to The Royal Marsden in London after a clinical trial gave her renewed hope following a devastating cancer diagnosis. Rose was diagnosed with rare medullary thyroid cancer in 2020, after initially putting the back pain she experienced while training for a half-marathon down to wear and tear from an earlier hip replacement. Months later, discovering a lump in her neck led to the diagnosis that changed her life. Her cancer had already spread to her adrenal glands and liver when she was referred to The Royal Marsden. With limited treatment options available, Rose was offered a place on a clinical trial in May 2021. She chose to take the opportunity, and within six months, her tumours had shrunk by 60%. She remains on the medication and says scans continue to bring encouraging results.How cancer diagnosis changed Roseâs lifeRose first noticed something was wrong in March 2020 while training for a half-marathon. Back pain began interfering with her running, but because she had previously undergone a hip replacement, she initially believed the discomfort was simply related to her old injury. The situation became much more serious when she later discovered a lump in her neck. According to Just Giving, doctors diagnosed her with medullary thyroid cancer, a rare form of thyroid cancer that develops in the thyroid's specialised C cells. For Rose, the diagnosis was particularly frightening because she had three children and a partner. She described the moment as one in which her âworld just stoppedâ, as the family faced the uncertainty surrounding an advanced cancer diagnosis. By the time she reached The Royal Marsden, the cancer had spread to her adrenal glands and liver. Her treatment choices were limited, but she was offered an opportunity that could potentially change the course of her illness.The clinical trial that changed her outlookRose became one of a small number of patients in the UK given access to the clinical trial. She said there were only around nine or 10 places available nationally, making the opportunity particularly significant. Faced with the choice between an older drug that she feared would make her feel unwell and the new treatment being investigated through the trial, Rose decided to take what she described as a gamble. She began the new medication in May 2021 and has continued taking it. The results have given her reason to be optimistic. Within six months, her tumours had shrunk by 60%, while subsequent scans have continued to bring good news. Rose said some of her tumours have completely disappeared and that she feels well while taking the drug. Her experience also demonstrates why clinical trials are an important part of cancer research. Trials allow researchers to investigate treatments that may eventually provide additional options for patients whose cancers are difficult to treat.From cancer treatment to a 186-mile fundraising challengeAfter receiving treatment, Rose returned to cycling and decided to turn the activity into a personal tribute to the medical team that helped her. She began her 186-mile journey in Bridgwater and planned to finish at The Royal Marsden in London. The challenge combines something she loves with her desire to support the institution that played such an important role in her treatment. Rose has previously taken part in the London to Paris Cycle, but this ride carries a much more personal meaning. Rather than simply completing another endurance challenge, she is cycling towards the hospital where she received treatment and where research continues into advanced thyroid cancers. She said she wanted to make the journey personal because of the positive results she has continued to receive from her scans. Her fundraising will support The Royal Marsden's work, including research aimed at improving cancer diagnosis and developing more personalised treatments.Why cancer research matters beyond one patientThe Royal Marsden has played a leading role in research into advanced thyroid cancers, with clinical trials exploring new approaches to treatment. Rose's story illustrates the human impact that such research can have when experimental treatments eventually provide patients with new possibilities. For her, the ride is an opportunity to acknowledge the doctors, nurses, researchers and support staff involved in her care while helping fund future work. Antonia Dalmahoy, managing director of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, told BBC that Rose's fundraising would contribute towards research focused on earlier cancer diagnosis and better, more personalised treatments for patients in the UK and around the world. Rose's journey is therefore about more than the distance covered on a bicycle. It represents the years between a frightening diagnosis and a future she can once again plan for. After being told she had advanced cancer, she now has the chance to cycle towards the hospital that helped give her that future back.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Zambia elections: Courts sealed as election petition deadline looms
articles.summary: Preparations for President Hakainde Hichilema's second inauguration appear to be continuing.
articles.body:
Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches.

An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access.

Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%.

Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others.

Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September.

On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart.

One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area.

The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts.

It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment.

Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons".

The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation.

Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary.

A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition.

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) said it was concerned by the closure of the courts and the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises in Lusaka.

It said there was no formal public explanation for the closure nor its expected duration.

Referring to the "unsigned memorandum" from the judiciary addressing staff, it said no further official information had been provided to lawyers and the public.

"The closure of the courts has immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for persons requiring urgent judicial intervention," it said in a statement

It said the timing was "particularly significant in the present electoral context", citing a "seven-day period" in which a person may "petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect".

Despite the court closure, preparations for Hichilema's inauguration appear to be continuing.

The youth and sport ministry has issued a media invitation for journalists to accompany a cabinet official on an inspection of arrangements at National Heroes Stadium, where the ceremony is expected to take place.

Mundubile last week rejected the presidential election results and said he planned to challenge the outcome through the courts.

He remains in a secure location under the protection of what his campaign describes as an "international human rights body".

He went into hiding after the arrests of opposition figures and the death of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a raid by security officers, in what officials described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital.

The arrests as well as the death of Kafwaya prompted calls from rights groups and the Law Association of Zambia for an independent investigations.

Amnesty International described the Kafwaya's killing as "deeply alarming" and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations. The lawyers' association similarly expressed "grave concern" and demanded investigation.

The election day, 13 August, was described by regional and international observers as largely peaceful, but they raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll.

The EU observation mission said restrictions on the opposition may have contributed to an "uneven contest".

On vote tallying, the mission described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres.

It said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters.

The EU mission also called for "maximal transparency" over the poll outcome, noting that the electoral commission did not publish separate polling-station results
